prompt:
Each item below is a decision point in an AI-safety research project. You get the kind of decision, a short statement of the problem the team faced, and the text of their write-up that comes BEFORE the decision. You do not see what they decided, and you must not guess it.

For each item write the decision point as a researcher would have faced it, BEFORE choosing:
- "context": 2-4 sentences, neutral third person ("A research team ..."). The setting, what they were studying, and what they knew at that moment; for a decision about interpreting, accepting or stating a result, the result itself. Give the facts that any reasonable option would need. The excerpt may already announce or describe what the team chose (papers often state their choices before explaining them): leave all of that out. Do not list candidate options, do not mention methods or elements the team adopted as part of this decision, and do not say anything learned after it.
- "question": one short open question naming the decision, answerable in several different ways, e.g. "How should the team test whether the effect depends on the clean data?" It must not suggest an answer.
- "skip": true if the decision cannot be posed without stating its outcome, or is not a real choice (pure description). Otherwise false.
No names of people, labs, organisations, papers, models or datasets; no coined name for the phenomenon (describe it in plain words). Numbers are fine.

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "skip": bool, "context": str, "question": str}]}

ITEMS:

This is a revision. Each item also shows your previous context and question. Readers who knew what the team decided found that this version steers toward one particular resolution: it states or implies it, mentions elements that only one resolution would use, or frames the question so that one resolution is the obvious answer. You are still not told the decision. Rewrite the context and question so that several genuinely different resolutions answer the question equally directly: keep the facts any option needs, present facts that cut different ways neutrally, drop details that only matter to one particular resolution, and invent nothing.

=== key f1f87537c4b7
Kind of decision: how to interpret an ambiguous result
Problem: Whether the question of whether transformers 'truly' do mesa-optimization is meaningful
Write-up text before the decision: timization](/api/post/FkgsxrGf3QxhfLWHG) mesa-optimization is characterized as *[...] it is also possible for a neural network to itself run an optimization algorithm. For example, a neural network could run a planning algorithm that predicts the outcomes of potential plans and searches for those it predicts will result in some desired outcome. Such a neural network would itself be an optimizer because it would be searching through the space of possible plans according to some objective function. If such a neural network were produced in training, there would be two optimizers: the learning algorithm that produced the neural network—which we will call the base optimizer—and the neural network itself—which we will call the mesa-optimizer.* In this definition, the question of whether a network performs mesa-optimization or not boils down to whether whatever it does can be categorized as optimization, planning or search with an objective function. We think this question is very hard to answer for most networks and ML applications in general, e.g. one could argue that sparse linear regression performs search according to some objective function and that the attention layer of a transformer implements search since it scans over many inputs and reweighs them. We think this is an unhelpful way to think about transformers but it might technically fulfill the criterion. On the other hand, transformers very likely can’t perform variable length optimization like tree search or a recursive optimization procedure. Thus, they are not able to perform many forms of optimization.
Previous context: A research team is examining a standard definition under which a network counts as performing internal optimization if it runs search or planning according to an objective function. They observe that this criterion is very hard to apply: sparse linear regression or a transformer's attention layer could arguably satisfy it, which they find unhelpful, while transformers also plausibly cannot perform variable-length or recursive optimization procedures.
Previous question: Should the team treat the question of whether transformers 'truly' perform internal optimization as meaningful and answerable, or reframe it?

After sharing our updated compute trends analysis a common question was: "*So how are your findings different from* [*OpenAI’s previous compute analysis*](https://openai.com/blog/ai-and-compute/) *by Amodei and Hernandez?*". We try to answer this question in this short post. Comparison to OpenAI’s AI and Compute ------------------------------------- [OpenAI’s analysis](https://openai.com/blog/ai-and-compute/) shows a 3.4 month doubling from 2012 to 2018. Our analysis suggests a 5.7 month doubling time from 2012 to 2022 (Table 1, *purple*). In this post, we investigate this difference. We use the same methods for estimating compute for the final training run. Our methods are described in detail in [*Estimating training compute of Deep Learning models*](/api/post/HvqQm6o8KnwxbdmhZ). Our analysis differs in three points: (I) number of samples, (II) extended time period, and (III) the identification of a distinct large-scale trend. Of these, either the time period or the separation of the large-scale models is enough to explain the difference between our results.
